newsitem.title: USA: Dow hits 6,900 and tumbles; dollar near 4-year top.
newsitem.headline: Dow hits 6,900 and tumbles; dollar near 4-year top.

text.p: The Dow Jones industrial average closed sharply lower Thursday on the largest trading volume ever after rising above the 6,900 level for the first time.
The dollar rose to a 47-month high against the Japanese yen on reports suggesting that Washington wishes to strengthen the dollar. Bonds fell after an uneventful five-year Treasury note auction.

The Dow ended down 94.28 points, or 1.38 percent, at 6,755.75, dropping more than 150 points in the last two hours of trading as the barometer of 30-blue-chip stocks quickly retreated from a high of 6,906.60.

In the broader market, declining issues led advances 1,402 to 1,129 on trading of 683 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange -- the largest volume ever, beating the old record of 680 million set on July 16, 1996, the day after the Dow lost 160 points.
Analysts said the market's sudden turnaround resulted from a rapid sequence of sell programs apparently triggered by a downdraft in the Standard & Poor's 500 index futures market.

At the height of the session's rally, just as the Dow was surpassing 6,900 points, the S&P's futures contract was also nearing a key psychological level, said Mike Rothberg, managing director of portfolio trading at Cantor Fitzgerald.
"The (futures) contract got to an all-time high and was headed for 800," Rothberg said. "It hit 799.70 but couldn't break through and right after it turned around we had sell programs."
Hit hardest were many of the big-name stocks that had paced the Dow's seemingly unstoppable run toward 7,000.

"This was more than profit-taking," said Scott Bleier, chief investment strategist at Prime Charter Ltd. "These could be construed as major reversals, particularly because they were on such heavy volume."
However, he noted, that even after the sell-off, stocks are well higher than where they were at the start of the year.
"The caveat is that these stocks had massive runs before today," Bleier said.
Ironically, the selling pressure came as reports emerged that investment strategist Elaine Garzarelli had turned bullish on U.S. stocks, reversing her call for a 10 percent to 15 percent correction.
According to market sources, Garzarelli expects U.S. stocks to gain 10 percent to 15 percent in the next 12 months.

In the bond market, the bellwether 30-year Treasury bond fell 9/32, or $2.8125 on a $1,000 bond, sending its yield up to 6.86 percent from 6.83 percent at Wednesday's close. The bond's price and yield move in opposite directions.
The dollar rose to a 47-month high of 119.69 yen, before settling at 119.31 yen in late trading, above 119.03 yen late Wednesday.
The German mark rebounded, pushing the dollar to a session low of 1.6342 marks before it stablized. The dollar ended at 1.6325 marks, off from 1.6421 marks late Wednesday.
Coffee prices extended a dizzy rally fed by supply worries as the market hit its highest levels in 16 months.

On New York's Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange, March delivery coffee ended 4.75 cents higher at 140.05 cents a pound after surging to a new life-of-contract high of 142.00 cents, the highest price for coffee on weekly charts since September 1995.

At the Chicago Board of Trade, March corn closed 1/4 cent a bushel lower at $2.70-1/4 and March wheat 3-1/2 cents a bushel lower at $3.75-3/4 as the outlook for exports weakened due to strong overseas competition.

Overseas, London's FTSE 100 index finished at a record high for the fifth time this year, gaining 52.4 points to 4,271.5. In Tokyo, the Nikkei 225 was down 104.42 points, or 0.58 percent, at 17,909.46.
